title: Go Interfaces: The Complete Field Notes
summary: A dense ten-chapter handbook on Go interfaces — from implicit satisfaction and method-set rules to iface/eface internals, embedding, type assertions, type switches, and the design patterns and gotchas that bite in production code.

chapters.title: 1. What an Interface Actually Is
points: Definition: an interface type is a named set of method signatures — `type Stringer interface { String() string }`
An interface value is a variable whose static type is the interface; it can hold any concrete value whose method set includes those methods
Interfaces specify behavior, not data: no fields, no state, no implementation body
Method signature = name + parameter types + result types; no parameter names required in the declaration
Empty interface `interface{}` has zero methods, so every type satisfies it; `any` is an alias for it since Go 1.18
The zero value of an interface is `nil` — both its type and value words are unset
Calling any method on a nil interface panics: `runtime error: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference`
Interfaces are types, so they work anywhere a type works: parameters, returns, struct fields, map values, slice elements
`var w io.Writer = os.Stdout` — assignment is where satisfaction is checked, at compile time
Go interfaces are structural (shape-based), unlike Java/C# nominal interfaces that require a declared `implements`
Interface method sets are unordered sets — declaration order in the interface has no meaning
Duplicate method names in one interface literal are a compile error; overlapping methods from embedded interfaces are allowed if signatures are identical (Go 1.14+)
Canonical stdlib examples: `error` (one method `Error() string`), `fmt.Stringer`, `io.Reader`, `io.Writer`, `sort.Interface`
Interfaces are the only form of dynamic dispatch in Go — no classes, no inheritance, no virtual functions

chapters.title: 2. Implicit Satisfaction
points: No `implements` keyword: a type satisfies an interface simply by having the required methods
Satisfaction is checked by the compiler at assignment/conversion/call sites, not at type declaration
Consequence: you can write an interface *after* the concrete types exist, and retrofit stdlib or third-party types you don't own
Consequence: the consumer package defines the interface, so producers need no import of the consumer — dependency arrow flips
`var _ io.Writer = (*MyType)(nil)` — the compile-time assertion idiom, costs nothing at runtime, fails the build if the type drifts
Method name and full signature must match exactly; a differing parameter or return type means no satisfaction
Typical error message: `cannot use x (variable of type T) as io.Writer value: T does not implement io.Writer (missing method Write)`
The wrong-signature error is more subtle: `have Write([]byte) int` / `want Write([]byte) (int, error)`
Unexported methods can only be satisfied from inside the declaring package — used to seal an interface (e.g. `testing.TB`)
Accidental satisfaction is real: any type with `String() string` becomes a `fmt.Stringer` and changes how `fmt` prints it
Interfaces can be satisfied by any named type, not just structs: `type Celsius float64` with a `String()` method works
Function types satisfy interfaces too — `http.HandlerFunc` is a func type with a `ServeHTTP` method (the adapter pattern)
Duck typing with static checking: shape-based like Python, but every mismatch is caught at compile time
The stdlib leans on this heavily: `io.Copy` works with files, sockets, buffers, and gzip streams that never knew about each other

chapters.title: 3. Method Sets: The Core Rule
points: Method set = the set of methods callable on a value of a given type — it determines interface satisfaction
Rule for value type T: method set contains only methods declared with receiver `T`
Rule for pointer type *T: method set contains methods with receiver `T` AND receiver `*T`
So *T satisfies strictly more interfaces than T; T never satisfies more than *T
Why: the compiler can always take the address of what a pointer points to, but cannot always address an arbitrary value
Method values on addressable variables: `v.PtrMethod()` compiles because Go rewrites it as `(&v).PtrMethod()` — this is sugar, not method-set membership
That sugar does NOT apply to interface satisfaction: `var i I = v` fails even though `v.PtrMethod()` compiles
Error to memorize: `T does not implement I (method M has pointer receiver)`
Non-addressable values can't even use the sugar: map elements `m[k].PtrMethod()` is a compile error — copy to a variable first
Values returned from function calls are non-addressable: `f().PtrMethod()` fails the same way
Embedded field promotion follows the same rules: embedding T into S promotes T's value methods to S and *S; embedding *T promotes both sets to S and *S
Interface types have method sets equal to their declared methods — an interface never gains pointer-receiver privileges
Reflection view: `reflect.TypeOf(v).NumMethod()` vs `reflect.TypeOf(&v).NumMethod()` shows the split concretely
Practical rule: keep the receiver kind consistent across all methods of a type, and pass `&v` when in doubt

Table row — Value receiver + value var: methods OK, interface OK. Value receiver + pointer var: methods OK, interface OK. Pointer receiver + value var: methods OK (if addressable), interface FAIL. Pointer receiver + pointer var: methods OK, interface OK

chapters.title: 4. Pointer vs Value Receivers
points: Value receiver `func (c Counter) Get() int` operates on a copy — mutations are discarded
Pointer receiver `func (c *Counter) Inc()` operates on the original — mutations persist
Classic bug: `func (c Counter) Inc() { c.n++ }` compiles, runs, and silently does nothing
Choose pointer receiver when: the method mutates, the struct is large, or the type contains a `sync.Mutex` or other no-copy field
Choose value receiver when: the type is small and immutable-ish (time.Time, small structs, named scalars), or you want the value to be safely copyable
Copying a struct that embeds `sync.Mutex` by value copies the lock state — `go vet` flags this via the copylocks check
Don't mix receiver kinds on one type: it confuses the method set and makes satisfaction depend on how the variable was declared
Slices and maps are reference-like headers, so a value receiver can still mutate the backing array or map entries — but cannot `append` visibly
`append` inside a value receiver updates only the local slice header; the caller sees the old length
Method values capture the receiver at bind time: `f := v.Get` copies v for a value receiver; `f := p.Inc` captures the pointer
Cost model: value receivers copy the struct on every call; pointer receivers copy one word but may push the value to the heap (escape analysis)
`go build -gcflags=-m` reveals `moved to heap` decisions caused by pointer receivers escaping into interfaces
The `error` convention: implement `Error() string` on `*MyError` and return `&MyError{}` so equality and mutation behave predictably
Sentinel counter-case: small immutable error types with value receivers let `errors.Is` compare by value
Rule of thumb from the stdlib: if any method needs a pointer receiver, give every method a pointer receiver

chapters.title: 5. Interface Internals: iface and eface
points: An interface value is a two-word struct: (type descriptor pointer, data pointer) — 16 bytes on 64-bit
Non-empty interfaces use `iface{ tab *itab, data unsafe.Pointer }`
Empty interfaces use `eface{ _type *_type, data unsafe.Pointer }` — no method table needed
The `itab` holds: the interface type, the concrete type, a type hash, and an array of method function pointers
itabs are built once per (interface, concrete type) pair and cached in a global hash table — dispatch itself is just a load + indirect call
Method call `w.Write(b)` compiles to: load `tab.fun[i]`, call it with `data` as the receiver
Storing a value in an interface copies it; if it doesn't fit in a pointer word it is heap-allocated first
Since Go 1.4 the data word is always a real pointer — no more small-value inlining into the word
Common optimization: small integers 0–255 and the empty string reuse `runtime.staticuint64s` / static storage, avoiding an allocation
This boxing is why `fmt.Println(i)` with an int can allocate, and why hot loops avoid `interface{}` parameters
The nil-interface trap: an interface holding a nil *T has a non-nil type word, so `i != nil` is true — the #1 Go gotcha
Rendered as a diagram: `iface -> itab -> {inter, _type, fun[0..n]}` alongside `iface.data -> concrete value`
Devirtualization: the compiler can inline an interface call when it proves the concrete type at the call site (PGO improves this since Go 1.21)
Type assertions compare the stored type descriptor pointer (or hash) — cheap, but not free
`unsafe`-based inspection or `runtime` source (`runtime/iface.go`) is the ground truth if you need to verify layout

chapters.title: 6. Embedding: Interfaces in Interfaces, Types in Structs
points: Interface embedding: `type ReadWriter interface { Reader; Writer }` unions the method sets
`io.ReadWriteCloser` composes three interfaces — the stdlib's standard composition ladder
Since Go 1.14 overlapping method names across embedded interfaces are legal if the signatures are identical
Struct embedding: `type Server struct { *log.Logger }` promotes the embedded type's methods to the outer type
Promotion is a compiler-generated forwarding method, not inheritance — there is no virtual dispatch to the outer type
Consequence: an embedded method calling another method gets the *embedded* type's version, never an outer override (no polymorphic self)
Embedding an interface in a struct gives partial implementation: unimplemented methods compile but panic at call time
That pattern powers forward-compatible wrappers, e.g. embedding `io.Reader` to override only `Read`
Ambiguity rule: at the same depth, two identically named promoted methods cancel out — the selector is a compile error unless you qualify it
Shallower depth wins: an outer method with the same name shadows the promoted one, which is how you override
Explicit access to the shadowed version: `s.Logger.Printf(...)`
The embedded field's name is its unqualified type name (`Logger` for `*log.Logger`, `Mutex` for `sync.Mutex`)
Embedding `sync.Mutex` gives the outer type `Lock`/`Unlock` — but exports them as part of your public API; prefer a named field if that's not intended
Composition over inheritance in practice: embed for reuse, define small interfaces for polymorphism
Decorator example: `type countingWriter struct { io.Writer; n int }` with a custom `Write` that increments and delegates

chapters.title: 7. Type Assertions and Type Switches
points: Single-value form `s := i.(string)` panics if the dynamic type doesn't match: `interface conversion: interface {} is int, not string`
Comma-ok form `s, ok := i.(string)` never panics; on failure `ok` is false and `s` is the zero value
Asserting to a concrete type asks 'is the dynamic type exactly T?'
Asserting to an interface type asks 'does the dynamic type implement I?' and yields an interface value
Asserting on a nil interface always fails (`ok == false`) — no panic in comma-ok form
Type switch syntax: `switch v := i.(type) { case int: ...; case string: ...; default: ... }`
Inside each single-type case, `v` has that concrete type; in a multi-type case `case int, int64:` v keeps the interface type
`case nil:` matches a nil interface value — distinct from a non-nil interface holding a nil pointer
Type switches are checked for duplicate cases at compile time; unlike expression switches there is no fallthrough
Feature detection idiom: `if wt, ok := w.(io.WriterTo); ok { return wt.WriteTo(dst) }` — how `io.Copy` picks a fast path
`errors.As(err, &target)` is the type assertion for wrapped error chains; `errors.Is` compares against sentinels
Cost: an assertion to a concrete type is a pointer compare; to an interface it may need an itab lookup (cached, but not zero)
Overuse smell: a long type switch over your own types usually means you should have added a method to an interface
Legitimate uses: decoding `any` from JSON, feature/capability upgrades, error inspection, and reimplementing generic-ish helpers
Type parameters (generics, Go 1.18+) replace many `interface{}` + assertion patterns with compile-time safety

chapters.title: 8. Design: Small Interfaces, Right Placement
points: Proverb: 'The bigger the interface, the weaker the abstraction' — Rob Pike
Proverb: 'Accept interfaces, return structs' — flexible input, concrete and inspectable output
Define interfaces in the consuming package, not alongside the implementation — this is the opposite of Java convention
Single-method interfaces dominate the stdlib: `Reader`, `Writer`, `Closer`, `Stringer`, `error`, `sort.Interface` is the fat outlier at three
Naming convention: single-method interfaces take the method name plus `-er` (`Reader`, `Formatter`, `Notifier`)
Don't create an interface until you have a second implementation or a real test seam — premature interfaces add indirection with no payoff
Interface pollution: mirroring every struct with a same-shaped interface makes navigation and refactoring worse
A one-method seam is trivially mockable without a mocking framework — just a func-typed adapter
`io.Copy(dst Writer, src Reader)` is the canonical payoff: one function, unlimited combinations
Middleware pattern: `func Logging(next http.Handler) http.Handler` composes because `Handler` is one method
Capability upgrade pattern: define the small interface, assert for the bigger one at runtime (`io.ReaderFrom`, `http.Flusher`)
Table: Go — implicit, consumer-defined, small; Java/C# — explicit `implements`, producer-defined, often wide; Rust traits — explicit `impl`, can be added to foreign types, static dispatch by default
Interfaces vs generics: use an interface when behavior varies at runtime; use a type parameter when the type is known at compile time and you want no boxing
Testing: a small interface plus a hand-written fake beats a generated mock for readability in most Go codebases
Documenting an interface should describe the contract (blocking? reentrant? who closes?), because the compiler only checks shape

chapters.title: 9. Costs, Trade-offs, and Performance
points: Interface method call = indirect call through the itab; typically a few ns, but it blocks inlining of the callee
The bigger cost is usually the lost inlining and the resulting escape-to-heap, not the indirect jump itself
Boxing: assigning a non-pointer concrete value to an interface may allocate; check with `-benchmem` and `-gcflags=-m`
Zero-cost cases: pointer values, small ints in the static cache, and values the compiler devirtualizes
`interface{}`-based containers cost an allocation per element plus an assertion per read — generics avoid both
Table row — direct call: inlinable, no allocation. Interface call: not inlinable (usually), possible boxing. Generic call: monomorphized per GC shape, often inlinable
GC pressure: many boxed small values means many tiny heap objects and more scanning work
Type assertion cost: concrete-type assertion is a single pointer comparison; interface-to-interface goes through `getitab` (cached)
Type switch with many cases compiles to a hash-based jump on the type descriptor, not a linear scan of every case
PGO (Go 1.21+) can devirtualize hot interface calls into direct, inlinable calls — measure before hand-optimizing
Avoid interfaces in the innermost loop of a hot path; hoist the assertion out of the loop instead
Benchmark shape: `func BenchmarkIface(b *testing.B)` comparing a direct call, an interface call, and a generic call on the same work
Don't preemptively de-interface: readability and testability usually outweigh single-digit-nanosecond dispatch cost
Interface comparison (`i1 == i2`) compares type and value; comparing interfaces holding uncomparable types (slice, map, func) panics at runtime
Interfaces as map keys inherit that hazard — `panic: runtime error: hash of unhashable type []int`

chapters.title: 10. Gotchas Checklist and Recap
points: #1 The typed-nil trap: `var p *MyErr; var e error = p; e != nil` is TRUE — never return a nil concrete pointer as an error interface
Fix for the typed-nil trap: return the literal `nil`, or check `if p != nil { return p }; return nil`
#2 Pointer receiver + value assignment: `var i I = v` fails — remember the method-set rule and assign `&v`
#3 Mutating in a value receiver: the change lands on a copy and disappears
#4 Range variable capture: `for _, v := range items { list = append(list, &v) }` — pre-Go 1.22 every pointer aliases the same variable
#5 Comparing interfaces holding slices/maps/funcs panics at runtime, even though the code compiles
#6 Accidental `Stringer`: adding `String()` silently changes `fmt` output everywhere; a `String()` that formats itself with `%v` infinitely recurses and stack-overflows
#7 Embedding an interface in a struct compiles with no implementation, then nil-panics when the missing method is called
#8 `errors.Is` vs `errors.As`: `Is` for sentinel identity, `As` for extracting a concrete error type from the chain
#9 Forgetting comma-ok on an assertion turns a recoverable mismatch into a panic
#10 Interface satisfaction drift on refactor — guard with `var _ I = (*T)(nil)` in every package that must satisfy something
Recap: interfaces are behavior sets; satisfaction is implicit and structural; method sets decide who satisfies what
Recap: values are two words (type + data); pointer receivers narrow the method set of T; embedding composes, it does not inherit
Recap: assertions and type switches recover the concrete type; keep interfaces small and define them where they're used
Cheat line: 'Pointer receiver? Pass a pointer. Small interface? Define it at the consumer. Nil error? Return literal nil.'
